Police Impersonation

By: Graham Coetzer | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take a look at the alarming rise in police impersonation cases in Gauteng, and ask what, if anything, can be done to stop this disturbing crime trend.

Unique Selling Point:
From "blue light" gangs, to scams and extortion, South Africa has seen an alarming increase in cases where criminals are impersonating police officers to get away with their crimes over the last few years. Gauteng is one of the provinces hardest hit by these types of crimes. Security experts say that they are seeing new cases on a weekly basis, and that multiple gangs, organised crime syndicates and even prisoners, who are currently incarcerated, are behind the crimes. And it's not just people dressed in police uniforms anymore, nowadays criminals even have access to sophisticated software which allows them to duplicate telephone numbers, making it seem as though they are calling you from legit law enforcement telephone numbers.

Summary:
After our last blue lights gang story aired last year, we were inundated by submissions from viewers who had similar experiences. In some of our latest cases, the MO seems to be almost identical, although attacks are happening all over Gauteng. In one interesting case, Chris Cronje was hijacked by men dressed as police officers who were driving a police vehicle. He was kept hostage for hours, as the hijackers drove around with him held at gunpoint in the back of the car, stopping at various ATM's and withdrawing an eventual total of R16k. He was later dropped off in a veld near Heidelberg. His vehicle was recovered two weeks later, near the Mozambican border - indicating it was most likely going to be shipped cross border. But the blue light gangs are not the only police impersonators doing the rounds. In the past year a new police impersonation scam, one that targets men who have visited sex workers or strippers, has become very popular. The men are contacted via whatsapp a day or two after their "meetings", and threatened by a man claiming to be a policeman. They are told the women they have met have laid charges of rape and/or assault against them, and the scammers demand amounts between R5000 and R50 000 to make the case "go away". The men are told that they will be arrested, not get bail, and of course warned of the disgrace of rape charges hanging over their heads. The tow truck scam, which we have featured before, also remains popular, as well as cases of extortion against business owners like restaurants, pubs and taverns, all targeted by men pretending to be police.

Further information:
We have very good case studies.

We have lots of actual cellphone images of arrests of police impersonators, which clearly show actual SAPS uniforms etc being used.

We have the whatsapp messages used in the rape scam against one victim.

The rape scam victim has agreed to talk to us with a hidden id

We have excellent security experts from a little known NPO who does amazing work in South Africa called Nationwide Crime SA. They are a group of hundreds of volunteers in the security, emergency services and police service who have agreed to work together as much as possible in combating crime. They deal with these types of cases very often, and have even traced one of the SAPS tow truck scammers back to a prisoner using a cellphone in the Kgosi Mampuru prison in PTA.

They have evidence of the technology used to "duplicate" cellphone numbers, so that it could look like real police numbers phoning you.

We will shoot dramatisations of a lot of the impersonators tactics.

Solomzi Ngonelo Rape Scam Victim
Erika da Cruz Tow scam victim

Script:


Police Impersonators
First Draft Script
10 March 2021

Voice
Last year we exposed a terrifying new method used by so called “blue light” hijacking syndicates. Not only were the criminals impersonating police officers to commit vehicle hijackings, but their victims were held at gun-point for hours on end, and forced to hand over their bank cards and ATM pin codes before being dropped off in the middle of nowhere.

Sound Up George Visser
So we gave them our pins, because they tell you they are going to send one guy now, to the bank, and if he doesn’t get money, they are going to shoot you.

Link Masa
But, it’s not just the notorious Blue Light gangs who are terrorising innocent victims. Cases where criminals impersonate police to rob or scam people out of their hard earned cash, and sometime even harm them, are quite common. And experts are saying, they are on the increase…

Voice
In some cases the criminals don’t even need to get hold of real police uniforms, in fact you’ll never even meet them face to face.

Link Masa
In a scam that’s become very popular in the criminal underworld recently, the scammers, pretending to be legitimate police officers, use all sorts of extortion tactics to force their victims into paying them tens of thousands of rands. Now if they don’t pay, they’re told they will face criminal charges for rape, or sexual assault.

Voice
The victims in this new twist are men who recently would have had dealings with sex workers or exotic dancers. This man asked us to hide his identity for fear of further victimization…let's call him Mr X. In 2019 he organised for two women to perform a striptease at a friend’s bachelor party. What was supposed to be an evening’s harmless fun turned into a nightmare …the ominous phone calls started a few days later.

Sound Up Mr X
Masa: How did this all start?

Mr X: Well this nightmare started in mid 2019, and I just got an anonymous call from someone pretending to be a warrant officer, who claimed that their was a rape case opened against me, and they needed R5000 to stay the prosecution.

Voice
He was completely innocent…its was a bogus charge, but for Mr X the consequences of even being associated with allegations of rape created real fear.

Sound up Mr X
And they are relentless in the sense of badgering and literally scaring you, to a point where you feel I’ve got nowhere to go but to pay.

Voice
After he paid the initial R5000, the fake cops kept demanding more money. In this whatsapp message Mr X was told he needed to pay an additional R12 000 to get the case removed from the court roll.

Sound Up Mr X
Masa: How legitimate do they sound for you to also get to the point of paying?

Mr X: They are legitimate in the sense that they’ve got your cellphone number, they know who you are, they know where you work. It sounds as if it’s somebody thats sitting in a police station.

Voice
The ordeal carried on…for close on a year! The scammers constantly applied pressure in messages like this one: “if they charge me you will also be charged with rape and bribing a police officer and this can take us to high court and media…”

Sound Up Mr X
I’d already been in the hole for about R30 000.

Voice
Mr X only discovered he was being conned after he enlisted the services of a private investigator.

The scam has added leverage on men who have broken the law by paying for sex. Former escort Anney spent 10 years as a sex worker. A few months ago her phone was stolen…and it wasn’t long before a man pretending to be a police officer began extorting her clients in this way - she was horrified.

Sound Up Anney
Well actually three of them actually cried, and begged me to withdraw the case, and I didn’t even know. They actually cried and I felt so sorry I didn’t know what they were talking about. There was a few that threatened me, to withdraw the case and I didn’t know what they were talking about.

Voice
Anney’s own digging led to the discovery that some sex workers sell their clients details to the syndicates behind the scams.

Sound Up Anney
I actually found out about one girl that actually sells her contacts to get money for them to commit the fraud. And I was shocked, wow.

Voice
Two men who deal with police impersonation cases on an all too regular basis are Craig Sacke and Richard Hoops.

Sound Up Craig Sacke
They are making money, so it’s increasing, without a doubt.

Voice
The former policemen who now own their own security companies, are also directors of a non-profit organisation called Nationwide Crime South Africa. Nationwide is a network of security companies, emergency medical services and police who have all agreed to assist each other in the fight against crime.

Sound Up Richard Hoops
It’s all about the passion of actually going out there and helping individuals out there, and it really is passion driven.

Voice
Sacke says their members respond to some form of a police impersonation case every other week, and have assisted in several arrests. According to him Gauteng remains a hotspot for the notorious blue light gangs.

Sound Up Craig
Especially with the truck hijackings, where the guys will follow them, blue lights in the dashboard, police uniforms.

Voice
These images are from a truck’s onboard cameras. The vehicle was allegedly hijacked by criminals dressed in police uniforms in December last year.

Sound Up Craig
The guys get out, hijack the trucks, only to be recovered later on with no loads.

Voice
Members of the public are targeted just as frequently. Chris Cronje from Kempton Park came face to face with a blue light gang when he was returning home from work on the N12 hi-way in February.

Sound Up Chris
And a police car came past me, and as they passed me they put lights on, the blue lights, and I though well whats this now. So eventually I slowed down and I stopped. And then I realised there was another car behind me also with blue lights.

Voice
Completely unaware of what was about to transpire, Cronje was casually searching for his driver’s licence when a man from the rear vehicle approached him.

Sound Up Chris
He was looking for drugs, and I said I don’t have drugs, and then he got quite aggressive, pointed the gun in my face and said you have to open the door. As soon as I opened the doors, other guys jumped into the car. And then they strangled me, pulled me through my car, through the door, into their car.

Voice
Cronje was held hostage in the back of the hijackers vehicle for what would become the most harrowing hours of his life.

Sound Up Chris
Chris: Tied me up, took my shoes, and took my jacket and put it over my face. And just drove off. And we were driving up and down, high speeds, screaming at me, obviously pointing the guns at me.

Masa: They’re holding you hostage for hours, what’s going through your mind, I mean you’ve got young boys at home?

Chris: You know, you think this is the end for me.

Voice
The gang also forced Cronje to hand over his ATM cards and pins.

Sound Up Cronje
And I gave him the pin code, and the one guy got very aggressive, he said I’m lying, swearing at me.

Voice
The hijackers kept Cronje hostage until after midnight, when his daily withdrawal limit reset, so that they could again draw cash from his ATM card, eventually ending up with R16 000.
His ordeal only came to an end when they dropped him off in the veld near Heidelberg.

Sound Up Chris
And they said I must get on my knees, and that’s also when I thought OK….you know because they were at the back of me, and it was quiet for like almost a minute and I didn’t know whats going to happen, are they going to shoot me now or what?

Voice
But the gang had sped off, netting his Lexus SUV and the cash. Craig Sacke says not everyone is that lucky.

Sound Up Craig
Leave him on the side of the road, maybe even shoot at him, kill him, and that’s basically how they do it.

Link Masa
You might be overjoyed when you find out that your stolen car has been found by police only a day after it went missing, but beware, if the police officer calling to give you the good news demands a payment for your vehicle to be towed, you’re being scammed.

Voice
Last year, we met Erika da Cruz, who had received such a phone call from police impersonators after her vehicle was stolen.

Sound Up Erika da Cruz
and he had indicated that he had found the vehicle in Komatipoort. They had arrested three suspects. He was very uncomfortable leaving the vehicle at the border. And this went on for about ten minutes, quite thorough, he had my case number, he knew what car I had, he had my name, my surname. I would have to pay the tow-truck driver R3200 to get the vehicle to Johannesburg.

Voice
The men phoning victims in these cases are not police and have not recovered any vehicles. They’re simply able to access vehicle registry databases through the criminal underworld.

Sound Up Craig
Masa: Now these guys are getting really sophisticated, it’s not just the uniforms, it’s also technology that they are using?

Craig: Yes, so one of the technologies that we’ve actually found is, it’s a software that you load on your phone, and they can basically mimic another person’s cellphone number.

Voice
And that gives the impersonator the terrifying ability to make it seem as if you’re being phoned from a legitimate law enforcement agency’s telephone number.

Sound Up Craig
So for example, we’re sitting here talking together, I could phone somebody else using your phone number, while you are sitting in front of me.

Voice
But until real cops can bring the impersonators to book, public confidence in the South African Police Service is fast being eroded.

Sound Up Chris
If it’s real cops and you are maybe driving away I don’t know they will start shooting at you because why are you not stopping, are you a criminal? And then you stop, and they hijack you… So it’s a very difficult thing.



Promo 1

From being hijacked and held hostage by blue light gangs to extortion rackets run by sophisticated syndicates, we take a closer look at the alarming spike in cases of police impersonations.

Promo 2

A new scam where men are threatened with charges of sexual assault unless they pay thousands of rands is just one example of a tidal wave of police impersonation crimes to hit our streets.

Promo 3

Hijackings, extortion and scams - we take a closer look at the inner workings of criminals gangs who are able to pull off their crimes by convincing innocent members of the public that they are police.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We take a look at the alarming rise in police impersonation cases in Gauteng, and ask what, if anything, can be done to stop this disturbing crime trend.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: From "blue light" gangs, to scams and extortion, South Africa has seen an alarming increase in cases where criminals are impersonating police officers to get away with their crimes over the last few years. Gauteng is one of the provinces hardest hit by these types of crimes. Security experts say that they are seeing new cases on a weekly basis, and that multiple gangs, organised crime syndicates and even prisoners, who are currently incarcerated, are behind the crimes. And it's not just people dressed in police uniforms anymore, nowadays criminals even have access to sophisticated software which allows them to duplicate telephone numbers, making it seem as though they are calling you from legit law enforcement telephone numbers.
metadata.Summary: After our last blue lights gang story aired last year, we were inundated by submissions from viewers who had similar experiences. In some of our latest cases, the MO seems to be almost identical, although attacks are happening all over Gauteng. In one interesting case, Chris Cronje was hijacked by men dressed as police officers who were driving a police vehicle. He was kept hostage for hours, as the hijackers drove around with him held at gunpoint in the back of the car, stopping at various ATM's and withdrawing an eventual total of R16k. He was later dropped off in a veld near Heidelberg. His vehicle was recovered two weeks later, near the Mozambican border - indicating it was most likely going to be shipped cross border. But the blue light gangs are not the only police impersonators doing the rounds. In the past year a new police impersonation scam, one that targets men who have visited sex workers or strippers, has become very popular. The men are contacted via whatsapp a day or two after their "meetings", and threatened by a man claiming to be a policeman. They are told the women they have met have laid charges of rape and/or assault against them, and the scammers demand amounts between R5000 and R50 000 to make the case "go away". The men are told that they will be arrested, not get bail, and of course warned of the disgrace of rape charges hanging over their heads. The tow truck scam, which we have featured before, also remains popular, as well as cases of extortion against business owners like restaurants, pubs and taverns, all targeted by men pretending to be police.
metadata.Further information: We have very good case studies. We have lots of actual cellphone images of arrests of police impersonators, which clearly show actual SAPS uniforms etc being used. We have the whatsapp messages used in the rape scam against one victim. The rape scam victim has agreed to talk to us with a hidden id We have excellent security experts from a little known NPO who does amazing work in South Africa called Nationwide Crime SA. They are a group of hundreds of volunteers in the security, emergency services and police service who have agreed to work together as much as possible in combating crime. They deal with these types of cases very often, and have even traced one of the SAPS tow truck scammers back to a prisoner using a cellphone in the Kgosi Mampuru prison in PTA. They have evidence of the technology used to "duplicate" cellphone numbers, so that it could look like real police numbers phoning you. We will shoot dramatisations of a lot of the impersonators tactics.
